content: The loss to follow-up after baseline was 20% or less. The quality rating of the study was Fair. Additional comments noted that if the quality was rated as Poor, reasons should be provided. For randomized controlled trials, the quality of random allocation concealment was assessed, with scores ranging from 2 (adequate concealment) to 0 (not adequately concealed or quasi-randomized). The comparability of groups at baseline was also evaluated, with scores ranging from 2 (comparable) to 0 (not comparable). Blinding of healthcare providers and outcome assessors was assessed, with scores ranging from 2 (blinding stated) to 0 (not blinded). Follow-up time was scored based on duration, with 2 indicating more than a year and 0 indicating no follow-up. The percentage of follow-up at the end of the trial was scored, with 2 indicating 60% or more and 0 indicating less than 40%. The total score determined the strength of the study, with scores above 15 considered strong, 10-15 moderate, and below 10 weak. The study by Manickam (2016) was a single-arm open-field trial aimed at determining the efficacy of preventing a 5-year cumulative 5% relapse rate, as well as assessing acceptability, safety, and compliance. Newly detected and untreated leprosy patients were enrolled from six centers in India and two centers in China between October 2003 and June 2008. After receiving U-MDT (Uniform Multidrug Therapy), patients were followed up for five years, with the last site completing follow-up in January 2014. A total of 3,437 patients were screened, and 3,389 were enrolled. The U-MDT regimen included supervised monthly doses of rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone, along with daily unsupervised doses of clofazimine and dapsone. Doses for children were slightly adjusted. Outcomes assessed included new lesions, relapses, reactions, disability, neuritis, and other events. Treatment was found to be acceptable across all centers, with no complaints about clofazimine pigmentation. The dropout rate at the end of the study was reported, with an initial sample of 3,389 and a final sample of 2,789. Follow-up duration was five years, with losses to follow-up described. The study by Penna (2012) was an open randomized controlled trial (RCT) that evaluated the association between treatment duration and the frequency of reactions in multibacillary (MB) leprosy patients. Patients were enrolled in the U-MDT/CT-BR program from March 2007 to February 2012. Statistical analyses included t-tests for continuous variables, chi-square tests for dichotomous variables, Kaplan-Meier methods for the frequency of first reactions, Poisson regression for recurrent reactions, and logistic regression to evaluate associations. The frequency of reactions was the dependent variable, with those experiencing no reactions serving as the control group. Follow-up was conducted, but dropout rates and losses to follow-up were not clearly described. The study by Penna (2014) was an open-label RCT that aimed to assess the association between treatment duration and trends in the bacilloscopic index (BI) over time among patients receiving U-MDT. Patients were enrolled in the U-MDT/CT-BR program from March 2007 to February 2012. The U-MDT regimen included six monthly supervised doses of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine, along with daily self-administered doses of dapsone and clofazimine for both MB and paucibacillary (PB) patients. Statistical analyses included linear regression and multilevel linear models with mixed effects. Follow-up duration was 24 months, with three follow-ups conducted at 12, 18, and 24 months. Dropout rates and losses to follow-up were described. The study by Prasad (2005) was a clinical trial that evaluated the clinical and histological advantages of adding clofazimine in PB patients. PB patients, classified according to WHO guidelines and confirmed smear-negative by slit-skin smear (SSS), were alternately allocated to MDT-PB or MDT-MB regimens between January 2001 and June 2002. Follow-up was conducted for one year, but details of dropout rates and losses to follow-up were not reported. The study by Rao (2009) was an open comparative study that assessed the efficacy, acceptance, and compliance of U-MDT. A total of 127 consecutive untreated PB and MB leprosy patients were alternately allocated into study and control groups between March 2003 and July 2005. Statistical analyses were not conducted due to the small sample size. Follow-up was conducted, but dropout rates and losses to follow-up were not clearly described. In summary, these studies evaluated various aspects of leprosy treatment regimens, including efficacy, safety, compliance, and outcomes such as relapse rates, reactions, and histological improvements. The quality of the studies varied, with some providing detailed follow-up data and others lacking clarity in reporting dropout rates and losses to follow-up.
